title: Finance and equipment serve different roles

blocks.heading: Finance and equipment serve different roles
blocks.text: Money capital finances the acquisition of resources; capital goods are produced assets used in production. A spending decision should address the actual bottleneck: additional equipment does not remove a shortage of materials or operating finance. An invented furniture group has a functioning saw and orders but no timber. Finance for timber could let the saw and workers produce saleable goods. Buying a second saw leaves the stated timber shortage unresolved. If the original saw were unusable instead, repair or replacement would be a different priority.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Money capital
blocks.text: Money capital is finance available to acquire resources for production; distinguish it from the productive equipment purchased. Spending available finance changes what resources are held; a cash balance and an acquired tool are not the same kind of input. N$900 held for purchasing material is money capital. It can finance materials, transport or equipment depending on the productive need. The cash cannot stitch a bag itself. Describe the financing role rather than calling every valuable possession machinery.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Capital goods
blocks.text: Capital goods are produced assets used to make other goods and services, such as tools, machinery and buildings. An asset’s productive use distinguishes it from finance and from a good used directly for final consumption. A sewing machine used to make bags is a capital good. Its price is not what gives it this role; it is a produced asset serving production. Equipment can become less useful if it breaks or no suitable operator, power supply or materials are available.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Choose finance or equipment by the bottleneck
blocks.text: A fictional repair group has usable tools, trained workers and confirmed work, but lacks N$600 to buy replacement components. Money capital for components would remove the immediate shortage. The tools are capital goods; the cash financing the purchase is money capital. Asking whether a resource finances an activity or performs productive work separates the concepts. The same amount of cash spent on another tool would not supply the missing components.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated

blocks.heading: Connect production to development
blocks.text: The factors-of-production lesson explains why inputs work together. Distinguish finance from equipment in every application; use the stated shortage to determine the purchase.
context_tags: original teaching; fictional examples where stated
